feedback: If a part reads 8p or 12.8p, check: do the four equal parts add back to £3.20? 80p × 4 = £3.20, so each quarter is 80p.
The 12.8p trap treats £3.20 as the bare number 3.2 and multiplies (3.2 × 4 = 12.8) instead of dividing; 'a quarter OF' makes the amount smaller, so you divide.
If 'a quarter' was treated as 25 of something, connect ¼ to one of four equal parts of this specific amount.
activities.intendedInsight: Finding a fraction of an amount is a division: a quarter of £3.20 is £3.20 shared into 4 equal parts, which is 80p.
learnerActions: Take a bar representing £3.20 and split it into four equal parts.
Read what one part is worth and label it (80p / £0.80).
Write the matching calculation: ¼ of £3.20 = £3.20 ÷ 4 = 80p.
Check by adding or multiplying back: 80p × 4 = £3.20.
State in your own words why 'a quarter of' means dividing by 4.
activities.title: Split the £3.20 bar: a quarter as division

feedback: If your answer is not 1.75 m, or does not match your ruler estimate, check whether 2.5 and 0.75 were lined up by their last digits instead of by the decimal point, and whether the exchange (borrowing) was done correctly.
Rewriting 2.5 as 2.50 does not change its value — it just makes the hundredths column visible for 0.75.
Compare your answer to the ruler: cutting a bit less than 1 m off 2.5 m should leave a bit more than 1.5 m and less than 2 m, so 1.75 m is sensible.
activities.intendedInsight: Decimals with different numbers of decimal places must be aligned on the decimal point before subtracting, because columns must match in place value; writing 2.5 as 2.50 is a helpful way to make the empty hundredths column visible.
learnerActions: Start with a 2.5 m rope marked on a ruler or number line.
Cut off 0.75 m and predict the remaining length before calculating.
Rewrite 2.5 as 2.50 so both numbers have the same number of decimal places.
Stack 2.50 above 0.75 with the decimal points lined up vertically, then subtract with borrowing.
Read the remaining length (1.75 m) and check it against your prediction on the ruler.
activities.title: Cut the rope: align the point before subtracting

feedback: If £3.20 is read as '3 pounds 2 pence', place coins: 2 tenths of a pound is two 10p coins = 20p.
If 2.5 m is read as '2 m and 5 cm', note that 5 tenths of a metre is 50 cm, since 1 m = 100 cm.
On the trap case, £3.5 is £3.50, because the 5 sits in the tenths place.
activities.intendedInsight: The digit after the decimal point is tenths of the unit, so the 2 in £3.20 is 20p and the 5 in £3.5 is 50p — not a separate whole number of the smaller unit.
learnerActions: Look at £3.20 and say what each digit is worth: 3 pounds, 2 tenths of a pound, and 0 hundredths of a pound.
State what the 2 is worth in pence (20p, not 2p) and justify it.
Discuss the trap case: does £3.5 mean 3 pounds 5 pence or 3 pounds 50 pence? Explain which is correct and why.
Model an amount with coins and notes to confirm the tenths of a pound are 10p coins.
Repeat for a length: in 2.5 m, the 5 is 5 tenths of a metre = 50 cm, not 5 cm.
activities.title: Read the money by place value

feedback: 80p is correct because £3.20 ÷ 4 = 80p; the 12.8p trap comes from treating £3.20 as the bare number 3.2 and multiplying (3.2 × 4 = 12.8) instead of dividing, and the 8p trap from dividing (3.2 ÷ 4 = 0.8) and misreading 0.8 of a pound as 8p rather than 80p.
For 2.50 − 0.75, align the points and exchange 1 one for 10 tenths: the answer is 1.75. A different result usually means the numbers were not lined up by the decimal point or the exchange went wrong.
0.3 kg = 300 g because 1 kg = 1000 g; 30 g or 3000 g uses the wrong power of ten.
activities.intendedInsight: These calculations are cleanly checkable, and the wrong options correspond to specific errors (money-as-two-numbers, misalignment, unit slips) worth recognising and avoiding.
learnerActions: Answer: what is ¼ of £3.20? (Correct: 80p / £0.80. The traps 8p and 12.8p are wrong.)
Match 0.3 kg to its equivalent in grams (300 g).
For each, briefly write the step you used so the method is visible, not just the answer.
activities.title: Quick checks on money, measure and conversion
